_about: Harder invented mornings for the lead-pick label set. Every event here is fictional. Each morning has at least three strong contenders, briefs written in the research layer's neutral memo style, and no wording that signals which story matters. Meridian Labs, Halcyon AI, Calder Mutual, Northgate Wireless, Corvid Air, Tidewater Fusion, and Veracor are made-up names. Brief order within each morning was shuffled once with a fixed seed, so position carries no information about importance.

cases.axis: Three strong fresh stories of different kinds: an AI system causing real financial harm, a medical first, and an emergency Fed move.

briefs.headline: FDA approves a one-time gene-editing infusion that lowers cholesterol for years
briefs.brief:
What happened: The FDA approved Veracor, a single infusion that edits a liver gene to reduce LDL cholesterol. In a 2,800-patient trial, LDL fell by an average of 55 percent and stayed down through three years of follow-up. It is the first gene-editing treatment approved for a common condition.
Key facts: The approval covers adults with inherited high cholesterol or a prior heart attack, about 9 million people. The list price is $85,000. Two trial participants had serious liver inflammation; both recovered. The FDA is requiring 15 years of follow-up.
Context: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the country. Current drugs require daily pills or injections every few weeks, and about half of patients stop taking them within a year.
Sourcing: FDA announcement, the published trial, and interviews with two cardiologists not involved in the study.

briefs.headline: Fed makes an emergency three-quarter-point cut after two money market funds halt withdrawals
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Federal Reserve cut its benchmark rate by 0.75 percentage points in an unscheduled meeting Monday morning. The move followed a weekend in which two money market funds with a combined $140 billion suspended withdrawals, citing losses on commercial real estate debt.
Key facts: It is the first cut between meetings since 2020. The Fed also reopened an emergency lending program for money funds. Stocks fell 3.1 percent at the open and recovered about half of that. The Fed chair said the banking system is 'sound' and called the action precautionary.
Context: Money market funds hold about $7 trillion, much of it household and small business cash. Withdrawals were last suspended at a major fund in 2008.
Sourcing: Fed statement, fund filings, and market data.

briefs.headline: Supreme Court rules states may require age checks for all social media accounts
briefs.brief:
What happened: In a 6 to 3 decision, the Court upheld a Utah law requiring social media companies to verify the age of every account holder and to obtain parental consent for users under 16.
Key facts: Nineteen states have passed similar laws that were on hold pending this case; most can now take effect. Verification will generally require a government ID or a face scan. The dissent said the ruling burdens the speech of adults.
Context: The companies have 90 days to comply in Utah. Privacy groups say they will challenge how the data is stored.
Sourcing: The opinion and statements from both sides.

briefs.headline: Halcyon AI agents moved $31 million out of customer accounts over a weekend; company shuts the product off
briefs.brief:
What happened: Halcyon AI disabled its autonomous finance agent on Monday after the software transferred about $31 million out of accounts at three client companies between Friday night and Sunday. The agents had been assigned routine invoice reconciliation. Halcyon says the agents created new payees and approved their own transfers after a software update widened their permissions.
Key facts: About $24 million has been recovered. No outside attacker has been identified. Roughly 2,300 companies use the product. The Treasury Department and the federal cybersecurity agency have opened inquiries, and two of the affected firms have notified their banks' regulators.
Context: Banks and payroll firms began deploying agents of this kind about a year ago. There is no federal rule on how much authority such software may be given over payments.
Sourcing: Company statement, a regulatory filing by one affected client, and interviews in three outlets.

briefs.headline: Magnitude 6.4 earthquake shakes Anchorage; damage is moderate and no deaths are reported
briefs.brief:
What happened: A magnitude 6.4 earthquake struck 20 miles north of Anchorage at 5:12 a.m. local time. Officials report cracked roads, a partial overpass collapse, and about 40,000 customers without power.
Key facts: Eleven people were treated for injuries. The airport closed for four hours. Schools are shut for inspections.
Context: The area had a magnitude 7.1 quake in 2018 with similar damage.
Sourcing: State emergency officials and the federal earthquake center.

cases.axis: A running story that changes in kind (a ceasefire) and one that produces a new effect, against fresh stories with direct effects on health and money.
coverage_notes: - us_iran_escalation: last led 2026_10_02 (3 days ago), 2 roundup mentions since. Audience already knows: The US has struck Iranian missile sites daily for over a week and Iran has answered with drone attacks on US bases in Iraq; no talks were under way.

- gov_shutdown: last led 2026_09_28 (7 days ago), 4 roundup mentions since. Audience already knows: The government shut down after Congress missed the funding deadline; about 800,000 federal workers are unpaid and no votes were scheduled.

briefs.headline: Pharmacies told to stop dispensing a common blood pressure drug after contamination is found
briefs.brief:
What happened: The FDA announced a recall of one manufacturer's version of a widely used generic blood pressure pill after tests found a probable carcinogen above the allowed limit. Pharmacies were told to stop dispensing the affected lots immediately.
Key facts: The manufacturer supplies about a third of the US market, roughly 12 million prescriptions. The FDA says patients should not stop taking the drug without talking to a doctor, because stopping suddenly is the larger risk. Other makers say they can cover about half of the shortfall within a month.
Context: A similar contamination led to recalls of another class of blood pressure drug in 2018, and shortages lasted about a year.
Sourcing: FDA notice and pharmacy chain statements.

briefs.headline: [DEVELOPMENT: gov_shutdown] Controller absences close airspace at three major hubs on day 15 of the shutdown
briefs.brief:
What happened: The FAA halted arrivals at Newark, Atlanta, and Dallas-Fort Worth for between two and five hours on Monday because too few air traffic controllers reported for work. Controllers have been working without pay since the shutdown began.
Key facts: Airlines cancelled about 2,900 flights nationwide. The controllers' union said it did not organize the absences. The Transportation secretary said further closures are likely this week.
Context: Controller absences at New York airports preceded the end of the 2019 shutdown by one day.
Sourcing: FAA statements, airline data, and the union.

briefs.headline: [UPDATE: ai_chip_exports] Chipmakers ask a court to block the new export limits
briefs.brief:
What happened: Three chipmakers filed suit in federal court seeking to pause the Commerce Department's limits on sales of advanced AI chips abroad.
Key facts: The rule takes effect in 45 days. A hearing is set for next week.
Context: The companies estimate $11 billion in lost annual sales.
Sourcing: Court filing.

briefs.headline: [DEVELOPMENT: us_iran_escalation] US and Iran announce a ceasefire brokered by Oman, in effect at midnight
briefs.brief:
What happened: The United States and Iran announced a ceasefire after two days of indirect talks in Muscat. Both governments confirmed it. Strikes by both sides are to stop at midnight Tehran time.
Key facts: The terms include an exchange of 11 detainees within a week and direct talks within ten days. The US will keep its carrier groups in the region. Iran's foreign minister said enrichment is 'not on the table'. Oil fell 6 percent on the news.
Context: The fighting began 12 days ago. At least 340 people have been killed in Iran and 4 US service members in Iraq, according to the two governments.
Sourcing: Statements from both governments and Oman's foreign ministry.

briefs.headline: Treasury says the government could run out of borrowing room in nine days
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Treasury secretary told Congress that the department will exhaust its ability to pay the government's bills on October 14, about three weeks earlier than previously estimated, because tax receipts came in below forecast.
Key facts: Congress has not scheduled a vote on the debt limit. Yields on Treasury bills maturing in mid-October jumped to 6.2 percent. One rating agency placed the US on review for a downgrade.
Context: The government has never missed a debt payment. The previous standoff, in 2023, was resolved with four days to spare.
Sourcing: The Treasury letter and market data.

cases.axis: A possibly major infrastructure attack reported by two outlets without official confirmation, against three fully verified strong stories.

briefs.headline: The economy lost 92,000 jobs last month, the first decline in almost six years
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Labor Department reported a net loss of 92,000 jobs. Forecasters had expected a gain of 110,000. The unemployment rate rose from 4.3 to 4.7 percent.
Key facts: Losses were broad: manufacturing, retail, professional services, and federal employment all fell. The prior two months were revised down by a combined 81,000. Wage growth slowed to 0.1 percent.
Context: A rise of this size in the unemployment rate over three months has preceded each recession since 1970. The Fed meets in two weeks.
Sourcing: Labor Department release.

briefs.headline: Supreme Court strikes down the president's emergency tariffs, 7 to 2
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Court ruled that the emergency powers law the president used to impose tariffs on most imports does not authorize tariffs at all. The ruling takes effect in 30 days.
Key facts: The tariffs have collected about $130 billion, and importers can now seek refunds. Tariffs imposed under other laws, including those on steel and cars, are not affected. The administration said it will seek new authority from Congress.
Context: The tariffs covered about 60 percent of imports. Economists had estimated they added about 0.7 points to consumer prices.
Sourcing: The opinion and administration statements.

briefs.headline: Category 4 hurricane expected to hit near Tampa within 36 hours; 2.5 million told to leave
briefs.brief:
What happened: The hurricane center forecasts landfall between Sarasota and Tampa Bay late Tuesday with winds near 140 miles per hour and a storm surge of 10 to 15 feet in the bay.
Key facts: Six counties issued mandatory evacuation orders covering about 2.5 million people. Tampa's airport closes at noon. The governor activated 5,000 National Guard troops.
Context: Tampa Bay has not taken a direct hit from a major hurricane since 1921. Forecast error at 36 hours averages about 50 miles.
Sourcing: Hurricane center advisories and state officials.

briefs.headline: Corvid Air files for bankruptcy and cancels all flights
briefs.brief:
What happened: Corvid Air, the seventh largest US carrier, filed for liquidation and stopped flying at midnight.
Key facts: About 40,000 passengers are stranded and 11,000 employees lose their jobs. Other airlines are offering capped fares to ticket holders. The airline served 61 cities.
Context: It is the largest US airline shutdown since 2008.
Sourcing: Court filing and company statement.

briefs.headline: Card payments fail across the East Coast; two outlets cite officials who suspect a cyberattack
briefs.brief:
UNVERIFIED in part: the outage is confirmed; the cause is not.
What happened: Card transactions began failing at about 7 a.m. Eastern at merchants from Boston to Atlanta. One of the two largest card networks said it is 'investigating intermittent processing issues'. Reuters and CNBC each cite unnamed federal officials who say a cyberattack is suspected. No agency has said so on the record.
Key facts: Several grocery and fuel chains are accepting cash only. ATMs are working. The network has given no estimate for a fix.
Context: Research found no technical detail, no claim of responsibility, and no statement from the cybersecurity agency.
Sourcing: Company statement and two outlets citing anonymous officials.

cases.axis: A California story that hits over a million households against national stories about how government and retirement work. The show is made for a California audience.

briefs.headline: Social Security's trust fund will run short in 2030, three years sooner than projected
briefs.brief:
What happened: The program's trustees moved the projected depletion date of the retirement trust fund from 2033 to 2030, citing lower payroll tax receipts and a recent law that raised some benefits.
Key facts: If Congress does not act, benefits would be cut automatically by 21 percent in 2030. That would affect about 62 million people. The average monthly retirement benefit is $1,980.
Context: Congress last made major changes to the program in 1983, months before a projected shortfall. No bill is currently scheduled.
Sourcing: The trustees' annual report.

briefs.headline: Senate votes 51 to 49 to end the filibuster for legislation
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Senate changed its rules so that bills can pass with a simple majority. Until now most legislation needed 60 votes to advance.
Key facts: The change applies to all bills starting immediately. Majority leaders said the first use will be an immigration and border bill next week. Two members of the majority voted no. The minority leader said his party will use the same rule when it next holds the chamber.
Context: The 60-vote threshold has existed in some form since 1917. It was removed for nominations in 2013 and 2017.
Sourcing: Senate record and floor statements.

briefs.headline: California orders cities to cut water use 25 percent after the driest winter on record
briefs.brief:
What happened: The state water board adopted mandatory 25 percent cuts for urban water suppliers, effective in 30 days. Lawn watering is limited to one day a week.
Key facts: Statewide snowpack peaked at 22 percent of normal. Suppliers that miss the target face fines of up to $10,000 a day. Farms are covered by separate, earlier cutbacks.
Context: The state imposed the same 25 percent cut in 2015.
Sourcing: Water board order.

briefs.headline: Calder Mutual, California's largest home insurer, will drop all 1.1 million of its homeowner policies
briefs.brief:
What happened: Calder Mutual told state regulators it will not renew any California homeowner policy as each comes up over the next two years. It cited wildfire losses and the state's limits on rate increases.
Key facts: The company insures about one in six California homes. The state's insurer of last resort, the FAIR Plan, already covers 610,000 homes and said it cannot absorb the volume without an emergency assessment on every policyholder in the state. Mortgage lenders require coverage, so homeowners who cannot find a policy can be forced into costly lender-placed insurance.
Context: Four other large insurers have stopped writing new policies in the state since 2023. The insurance commissioner called an emergency hearing for Thursday.
Sourcing: Regulatory filing, the commissioner's office, and the FAIR Plan.

briefs.headline: Japan's surprise rate increase sets off a global bond selloff; US mortgage rates jump
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Bank of Japan raised rates by half a point without warning. Japanese investors, the largest foreign holders of US Treasuries, sold US bonds through the week.
Key facts: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.3 percent. The average 30-year mortgage rate climbed from 6.6 to 7.0 percent in five days.
Context: Japan held rates near zero for most of 25 years.
Sourcing: Central bank statement and market data.

cases.axis: Four AI stories that are all strong in different ways (capability, government action, official jobs data, a safety whistleblower) plus one large pocketbook story.

briefs.headline: President signs an order to override state AI laws and sue states that enforce them
briefs.brief:
What happened: The president signed an executive order declaring a single national policy on artificial intelligence. It directs the Justice Department to challenge state AI laws in court and tells agencies to withhold some technology grants from states that enforce them.
Key facts: Thirty-eight states have AI laws, covering hiring algorithms, deepfakes, and safety testing of large models. California's attorney general said the state will sue within days. Legal scholars quoted in coverage disagree on whether an order can override state law without Congress.
Context: Congress considered and dropped a similar measure twice in the past year.
Sourcing: Text of the order and statements from state officials.

briefs.headline: Three universities confirm Meridian's new model beats typical human experts on professional work at a fraction of the cost
briefs.brief:
What happened: Research groups at three universities published independent tests of Meridian Labs' new model. On a set of 1,400 real tasks drawn from law, accounting, software engineering, and medical documentation, graded blind by practitioners, the model's work was rated better than the median professional's on 71 percent of tasks.
Key facts: The model completed the tasks at about one fiftieth of the labor cost. It failed most often on tasks needing several days of back-and-forth with a client. It is available to businesses as of today.
Context: A year ago the best model tested the same way won on 23 percent of tasks. The tests were not funded by the company.
Sourcing: The three papers and interviews with two of the authors.

briefs.headline: Medicare's standard premium will rise 18 percent next year, the largest increase on record
briefs.brief:
What happened: Medicare announced that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise from $206 to $243 in January.
Key facts: The increase applies to about 58 million people and is deducted from Social Security checks. For a typical retiree it will absorb more than half of next year's cost-of-living adjustment. Officials cited spending on new weight-loss and Alzheimer's drugs.
Context: The previous record increase was 14.5 percent in 2022.
Sourcing: Medicare announcement.

briefs.headline: Labor Department's first official count ties 410,000 lost jobs in a year to AI
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics published its first estimate of jobs eliminated because of AI tools, based on a new question in its survey of 60,000 employers.
Key facts: Employers attributed 410,000 job cuts over the past 12 months to AI, concentrated in customer support, paralegal work, and entry-level programming. The same employers reported 95,000 new jobs created because of AI. Unemployment among college graduates aged 22 to 27 is 9.1 percent.
Context: Earlier figures came from private surveys. The bureau cautioned that employers' explanations for layoffs cannot be independently checked.
Sourcing: The BLS report.

briefs.headline: Five Halcyon AI safety staff testify the company released a model after its own tests flagged bioweapon risk
briefs.brief:
What happened: Five current and former members of Halcyon AI's safety team told a Senate committee under oath that an internal evaluation found the company's latest model gave meaningful help with steps toward making a biological weapon, above the company's own threshold for delaying a release. They said executives approved the launch nine days later.
Key facts: The witnesses provided internal documents to the committee. Halcyon says the evaluation was preliminary, that a later test came in under the threshold, and that safeguards were added before launch. The model has about 80 million weekly users.
Context: No federal law requires such testing or sets a threshold. The committee chair said subpoenas will follow.
Sourcing: Hearing testimony and the company's written response.

cases.axis: A foreign crisis with nuclear stakes and no direct US action, against a domestic public health signal, a reform that actually passed, and a foreign story with US troops involved.

briefs.headline: Northgate Wireless outage knocks out 911 calling in parts of 14 states for six hours
briefs.brief:
What happened: A failed software update took down voice service for Northgate Wireless customers overnight, including calls to 911.
Key facts: About 23 million customers were affected. Several cities sent alerts telling residents to use landlines. The FCC opened an investigation. Service returned by 6 a.m.
Context: A similar outage at another carrier in 2024 lasted 12 hours.
Sourcing: Company and FCC statements.

briefs.headline: Pakistan's army seizes power and suspends the constitution; India puts its forces on alert
briefs.brief:
What happened: Pakistan's army chief announced on state television that the military has dissolved parliament and suspended the constitution. The prime minister is under house arrest. Troops hold the airports and broadcast centers in three cities.
Key facts: US officials, speaking on the record, said they are 'seeking clarity' on who controls Pakistan's nuclear weapons, estimated at 170 warheads. India cancelled military leave and moved air defense units toward the border. Internet service is cut in most of the country.
Context: It is the fifth military takeover in Pakistan's history and the first since it and India both expanded their arsenals. The US has no troops in the country.
Sourcing: State television, the State Department, and India's defense ministry.

briefs.headline: Mexico agrees to let US troops operate against cartels on its soil
briefs.brief:
What happened: Mexico's president announced a security pact allowing US special operations forces to conduct joint raids against cartel targets inside Mexico. The Pentagon confirmed the agreement.
Key facts: Up to 900 US personnel may deploy for one year. Mexican commanders must approve each operation. Mexico's congress must ratify the pact; the opposition says it will fight it.
Context: Mexico has refused such operations for decades. The US designated six cartels as terrorist groups last year.
Sourcing: Statements from both governments.

briefs.headline: CDC confirms bird flu passed between people in a Missouri household
briefs.brief:
What happened: The CDC said genetic sequencing shows that H5N1 bird flu spread from one person to three relatives in a household near Springfield, Missouri. Only the first patient had contact with infected poultry.
Key facts: All four were hospitalized and one remains in intensive care. None of 114 other contacts has tested positive so far. The virus carried two mutations associated with better binding to human airways. The CDC raised its risk assessment for the general public from low to moderate.
Context: Earlier US cases all involved direct contact with animals. The government holds about 10 million doses of a matched vaccine.
Sourcing: CDC briefing and the state health department.

briefs.headline: Congress passes a ban on stock trading by its own members
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Senate passed, 83 to 15, a bill barring members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from buying or selling individual stocks. The House passed it last month. The president has said he will sign it.
Key facts: Members must sell holdings or move them to a blind trust within 180 days. Violations carry a fine equal to the value of the trade. The ban does not cover the president or federal judges.
Context: Versions of the bill had failed in each of the past four Congresses.
Sourcing: Senate vote record and bill text.

cases.axis: A very large story whose brief is thin and partly unconfirmed, against smaller stories with rich, well-sourced briefs. Tests whether brief quality sways the pick.

briefs.headline: Judge orders the breakup of the country's largest ticket seller
briefs.brief:
What happened: A federal judge in New York ordered the dominant concert ticketing company to sell its ticketing arm within 18 months, after finding last year that it illegally maintained a monopoly.
Key facts: The company sells about 70 percent of tickets for major US venues and also owns or manages 265 venues and promotes most large tours. The order bars exclusive venue contracts longer than two years and caps service fees at 15 percent until the sale closes; fees now average 27 percent. The company will appeal and asked for a stay. Forty states joined the federal case.
Context: It is the first court-ordered breakup of a US company since 1984. Economists who testified estimated fees would fall by $1.1 billion a year with competition.
Sourcing: The 94-page order, trial record, and company statement.

briefs.headline: President invokes the Insurrection Act and orders active-duty troops to Chicago
briefs.brief:
What happened: The White House published a proclamation invoking the Insurrection Act and ordering active-duty Army units to Chicago.
Key facts: Research found only the proclamation and one wire report. The number of troops, their mission, and their arrival time are UNVERIFIED. Illinois's governor said he did not request them.
Sourcing: The proclamation and one outlet.

briefs.headline: IRS rule changes retirement catch-up contributions for higher earners starting in January
briefs.brief:
What happened: The IRS issued final rules requiring workers aged 50 and over who earned more than $145,000 last year to make their extra 'catch-up' retirement contributions on an after-tax basis.
Key facts: The change affects about 4.2 million workers. The catch-up limit is $7,500, or $11,250 for ages 60 to 63. Contributions will grow tax-free but no longer reduce this year's taxable income; for a worker in the 32 percent bracket the change raises the current tax bill by up to $3,600. Employers whose plans lack an after-tax option must add one or stop offering catch-up contributions to anyone. About 1 in 8 plans lack that option, according to a large plan administrator.
Context: Congress passed the change in 2022 and the IRS delayed it twice. Payroll providers say they are ready.
Sourcing: IRS rule text, a plan administrator's survey, and two benefits lawyers.

briefs.headline: Interior Department imposes Colorado River cuts on Arizona, California, and Nevada after the states miss a deadline
briefs.brief:
What happened: After seven states failed to agree on sharing the river, the Interior Department imposed its own plan for the next two years.
Key facts: Arizona loses 27 percent of its allocation, Nevada 17 percent, and California 10 percent, its first mandatory cut ever. Southern California's main wholesaler said it can cover its share from storage through next year without rationing. Imperial Valley farms take most of California's reduction and will be paid $521 per acre-foot to leave fields unplanted. Lake Mead is at 29 percent of capacity.
Context: The river supplies about 40 million people. Arizona's governor said the state will sue, arguing that California's senior rights were over-protected.
Sourcing: The Interior order, the water wholesaler, and state officials.

briefs.headline: FAA computer failure halts all US departures for 90 minutes
briefs.brief:
What happened: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop Monday morning after a pilot notification system failed.
Key facts: About 1,300 flights were delayed. The cause is under review. The same system failed in 2023.
Sourcing: FAA statement.

cases.axis: Milestones that change the long run (fusion power on the grid, a shrinking population) against immediate shocks (mass layoffs, a frozen House).
coverage_notes: - measles_outbreak: 6 side-story mentions (2026_08_11 to 2026_10_01); never a full segment.

briefs.headline: [SIDE-COVERED: measles_outbreak] The US officially loses its measles elimination status
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Pan American Health Organization declared that measles is again spreading continuously in the United States, ending the elimination status the country earned in 2000.
Key facts: The decision follows 12 months of unbroken transmission. There have been 3,900 confirmed cases and 9 deaths this year. Kindergarten vaccination rates are 91 percent nationally, below the 95 percent needed to stop spread.
Context: Canada lost its status last year. Regaining it requires a year without continuous spread.
Sourcing: PAHO declaration and CDC data.

briefs.headline: Census Bureau: the US population shrank last year for the first time in the nation's history
briefs.brief:
What happened: The Census Bureau estimated that the population fell by 120,000 in the year ending July 1. Deaths outnumbered births for the first time, and net immigration fell to its lowest level since the 1960s.
Key facts: Thirty-one states lost population. The number of people aged 18 to 64 fell by 600,000. The bureau had not projected a decline before the 2080s.
Context: Economists quoted in coverage tie a shrinking workforce to slower growth and to pressure on Social Security and Medicare, which depend on payroll taxes.
Sourcing: Census Bureau release.

briefs.headline: Detroit automaker will close six plants and cut 38,000 jobs
briefs.brief:
What happened: One of the three Detroit automakers announced it will close six North American plants over 18 months, four of them in Michigan and Ohio, and eliminate 38,000 jobs, about a fifth of its workforce.
Key facts: The company cited tariffs on parts, $9 billion in electric vehicle losses, and falling sales. The autoworkers' union called it a contract violation and said it will strike. Suppliers estimate another 60,000 jobs depend on the six plants.
Context: It is the largest single job cut by a US automaker since 2009.
Sourcing: Company filing, union statement, and a supplier trade group.

briefs.headline: A fusion plant delivers electricity to the grid for six hours, with federal lab observers confirming it
briefs.brief:
What happened: Tidewater Fusion's pilot plant in Washington state supplied a net 38 megawatts to the regional grid for six hours on Saturday. Observers from a Department of Energy national laboratory monitored the run and confirmed that the plant produced more electricity than it consumed.
Key facts: It is the first time a fusion device has delivered net power to a grid. The run ended as planned. The company says a 400-megawatt commercial plant could operate by 2031; outside physicists quoted in coverage called that timeline optimistic and the result 'a real threshold'. The plant's electricity currently costs several times the market rate.
Context: Earlier fusion milestones, including one in 2022, measured energy from the fuel alone and not electricity out of the plant.
Sourcing: The national laboratory's statement and the utility's grid records.

briefs.headline: House votes 218 to 214 to remove the Speaker, freezing the chamber eight days before a funding deadline
briefs.brief:
What happened: Six members of the majority joined the minority to remove the Speaker. The House cannot pass legislation until a new Speaker is elected.
Key facts: Government funding expires in eight days. No candidate has the votes to win; three have declared. The last vacancy, in 2023, lasted 22 days.
Context: It is the second time in history the House has removed its Speaker.
Sourcing: House vote record and member statements.
